title: Love brought back from ash
hook: Lalita wins her war, then brings Kama, love, back from the ash
carry: kama, love, is one of life's four aims
tomorrow: five things she does with the universe, and one of them is hiding

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama put four things in the goddess's hands: the noose that is desire, the goad that is anger, the bow that is the mind.

What happens to love after it's been burned to ash? In the old stories, Kama, the god of love, once aimed his flower arrows at Shiva in meditation. Shiva opened his third eye, and Kama was burned to nothing. The story told alongside the Lalita Sahasranama picks up from there. Tradition says something grew out of those ashes: a demon named Bhanda, who brought misery to the worlds until the gods offered themselves into a sacrificial fire and the goddess Lalita rose from it. Then comes a war, and the hymn, mostly names, tells the war in names too.
screen: `KAMA BURNED TO ASH.` → `A DEMON FROM THE ASHES.` → `A WAR TOLD IN NAMES.`

segments.voice: Read a stretch slowly and the story moves under the names like a river under ice. In paraphrase: she delights in the courage of her powers as they cut down Bhanda's army. She delights in the young goddess Bala, who strikes down Bhanda's sons. She glances at the face of Kameshvara, her consort, and from that glance Ganesha is formed. She rejoices when Ganesha shatters the device the demons built to block her army. Then the end: with Kameshvara's own weapon she burns Bhanda, and his city with him, and the gods praise her glory. A fine place to finish. But the hymn adds one more name, and it's the surprise. She is the life-giving herb for Kama, who was burned by the fire of Shiva's eye. After the battle, she brings love back. Hold that next to yesterday: Lalita carries the same sugarcane bow and flower arrows Kama carried. The hymn doesn't treat desire as an enemy to destroy forever. What grew wrong out of the ash is defeated, and the one who was burned is restored. Many teachers read Bhanda as desire gone wrong. It fits something Hinduism says plainly. The tradition names four aims of a human life: dharma, doing what's right; artha, a livelihood; kama, love and pleasure; and moksha, freedom. Kama is on the list. Wanting itself isn't the enemy. The hymn won't let a war be the last word about her. Healing is.
screen: `HER POWERS CUT DOWN BHANDA'S ARMY.` · `BHANDA AND HIS CITY BURN.` · `THEN SHE BRINGS KAMA BACK.` · `FOUR AIMS: DHARMA, ARTHA, KAMA, MOKSHA.` · then, large: `THE LIFE-GIVING HERB FOR KAMA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something in your life that once burned out, a friendship gone quiet, an old enthusiasm, a hope set down, and let it be there like ash after a fire. Without forcing anything, ask what small part of it might still be alive: a memory, a name, one phone number. If you pray, you can bring it before the goddess, or before God, in your own words; if you don't, let the question stay open.
The Lalita Sahasranama. A hymn of names that tells a war, and ends the war with Kama, love, brought back from ash.
Your line: kama, love, is one of life's four aims. She burned the demon and brought love back. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The story of Lalita's war with Bhanda is told in the Lalitopakhyana of the Brahmanda Purana, and devotees who recite the Lalita Sahasranama pass through the battle in a run of its names.

Story frame (Kama burned by Shiva's third eye; Bhanda arising from his ashes; the gods' sacrifice; Lalita rising from the fire) is from the Lalitopakhyana; Bhanda's origin is attributed as 'tradition says'. Confirm details, including the role of the gana Chitrakarma, deliberately left out.
Śūnyaka is Bhanda's city; 'burns Bhanda, and his city with him' paraphrases the name. Confirm.
Three readings (inward; story of restoring power; the order of the names) attributed to commentators and 'some readers' without naming one. Confirm fair.
The line 'the hymn won't let a war be the last word about her' refers only to this sequence; the hymn continues for many names after.
